14.details: First practical application of the て-form — this is the pattern students will use constantly to make requests. The すみませんが softener uses が as a connective in its weakened, non-contrastive 'softening remark' role, distinct from the true 'but' of S1が、S2.

14.title: V て-form います (be V-ing)
14.meaning: Indicates a certain action/motion is in progress — 'be V-ing.'
14.explanation: This sentence pattern indicates that a certain action or motion is in progress.

examples.jp: 田中さんは 今 電話を かけて います。
examples.en: Mr. Tanaka is making a phone call now.

examples.jp: 今 雨が 降って いますか。…はい、降って います。
examples.en: Is it raining now? …Yes, it is.

14.summary: Vて-form + います describes an action currently in progress ('is V-ing').
14.details: Second major use of the て-form. Note this is only one of several jobs ています will pick up: later points add a continuing-state meaning (結婚しています = 'I am married') and a habitual/occupational meaning (フィルムを 売って います = 'sells film [as a business]') — all sharing the same surface form but different meanings, worth reviewing as a set.

14.title: V ます-form ましょうか (Shall I...?)
14.meaning: Used when the speaker offers to do something for the listener.
14.explanation: This expression is used when the speaker is offering to do something for the listener.

examples.jp: 傘を 貸しましょうか。…すみません。お願いします。
examples.en: Shall I lend you an umbrella? …Yes, please.

examples.jp: 荷物を 持ちましょうか。…いいえ、けっこうです。
examples.en: Shall I carry your parcel? …No, thank you.

14.summary: Vます-form + ましょうか offers to do something for the listener ('shall I...?').
14.details: Distinct from Vましょう (proposing to do something TOGETHER) — ましょうか offers to do something FOR the listener, who isn't necessarily participating. Easy to conflate the two ましょう forms; worth a direct comparison drill.

14.title: S1が、S2 (introductory remark)
14.note: が used here as a light connective, not strictly contrastive.
14.meaning: が, having lost its original contrastive meaning, is used to lightly connect two sentences as an introductory remark.
14.explanation: The conjunctive particle が normally means 'but'. In expressions such as しつれいですが or すみませんが, which are used as introductory remarks when speaking to someone, が, losing its original meaning, is used to connect two sentences lightly.

examples.jp: 失礼ですが、お名前は？
examples.en: Excuse me, but may I have your name?

examples.jp: すみませんが、塩を 取って ください。
examples.en: Excuse me, but please pass me the salt.

14.summary: が in set openers like しつれいですが／すみませんが is a soft connective cushion, not the true 'but' contrast of S1が、S2.
14.details: Follow-up to contrastive S1が、S2 ('but'), clarifying that が has weakened here into a purely pragmatic cushioning device with essentially no contrastive meaning left. This is the same が seen in front of Vてください requests.

14.title: N が V
14.note: Natural phenomena take が as subject marker.
14.meaning: When describing a natural phenomenon, the subject is marked with が.
14.explanation: When describing a natural phenomenon, the subject is indicated by the particle が.

examples.jp: 雨が 降って います。
examples.en: It is raining.

14.summary: が marks the subject of natural-phenomenon sentences (雨が降ります, weather verbs).
14.details: Another が-as-subject-marker context, alongside preference/ability/existence verbs — natural phenomena are simply another category where が, not は, marks what's happening, since there's no 'topic' being discussed, just an event occurring.

14.title: Vます-form 方（かた）
14.explanation: Turns a verb into a noun meaning the way or method of doing it.

examples.jp: 漢字の読み方を教えてください。
examples.en: Please teach me how to read this kanji.

examples.jp: この機械の使い方が分かりません。
examples.en: I don't know how to use this machine.

14.summary: ます-stem + 方 means 'how to ~' (a noun for the method).
14.details: The pattern makes a noun, so it takes particles: 使い方が分かりません. The object of the original verb is marked with の, not を (漢字の読み方).

15.title: V て-form も いいです (You may do...)
15.structure: Vて-form も いいです／いいですか
15.meaning: Grants permission — 'you may do...'; the question form asks for permission.
15.explanation: This expression is used to grant permission. To ask for permission, the question form of this sentence is used. Note that an euphemistic answer is given when permission is not granted.

examples.jp: 写真を 撮っても いいです。
examples.en: You may take pictures.

examples.jp: このカタログを もらっても いいですか。…ええ、いいですよ。どうぞ。
examples.en: May I have this catalogue? …Yes. Here you are.

examples.jp: …すみません。ちょっと。
examples.en: …Sorry. I'm afraid not.

15.summary: Vて-form も いいです grants permission ('you may...'); Vて-form も いいですか asks for it; a refusal is often softened to すみません、ちょっと… rather than a flat no.
15.details: Builds directly on the て-form. Compare with Vてはいけません (prohibition) as the negative counterpart — Vてもいいです is the 'go ahead' side, Vてはいけません is the 'don't' side, and both attach to the same て-form.

15.title: V て-form は いけません (You must not do...)
15.structure: Vて-form は いけません
15.explanation: This sentence pattern is used to express prohibition. When you strongly wish to refuse permission to questions using the expression Vて-form も いいですか, you answer いいえ、いけません, omitting Vて-form は. This expression cannot be used by an inferior to a superior.

examples.jp: ここで たばこを 吸っては いけません。禁煙ですから。
examples.en: You must not smoke here. Because this is a no-smoking area.

examples.jp: 先生、ここで 遊んでも いいですか。…いいえ、いけません。
examples.en: May we play here, Ma'am? …No, you must not.

15.summary: Vて-form + は + いけません forbids an action ('must not'); a strong refusal can shorten to just いいえ、いけません; not used from a subordinate to a superior.
15.details: The negative-permission counterpart to Vてもいいです. Note the register restriction — like Vてください's superior-restriction, this can't be directed upward at a superior either, since it's a fairly blunt prohibition. Best learned as a matched pair with Vてもいいです.

15.title: V て-form います (continuing state)
15.note: Third use of ています, after the progressive — describes a resulting continuing state.
15.meaning: Describes a continuing state resulting from a past action — e.g. being married, knowing someone, living somewhere, possessing something.
15.explanation: In addition to the usage of an action in progress, Vて-form います is also used to describe a certain continuing state which resulted from a certain action in the past. もって います means 'be holding' and 'possess' as well.

examples.jp: わたしは 結婚して います。
examples.en: I'm married.

examples.jp: わたしは 田中さんを 知って います。
examples.en: I know Mr. Tanaka.

examples.jp: わたしは 大阪に 住んで います。
examples.en: I live in Osaka.

examples.jp: わたしは カメラを 持って います。
examples.en: I have a camera.

15.summary: Vて-form います can also describe a resulting ongoing state (結婚しています='I'm married', 知っています='I know', 住んでいます='I live', 持っています='I have/hold') rather than an action currently unfolding.
15.details: This is the second of ています's three meanings: progressive action vs. resulting state (here) vs. habitual/occupational — all identical in form, disambiguated only by the verb's inherent meaning and context. 知っています behaves specially — see 知りません for its irregular negative.

15.title: V て-form います (habitual action)
15.note: Fourth grammar sub-point but same て-form います surface pattern — habitual/occupational use.
15.meaning: Describes a habitual or repeated action performed over a period of time — including describing one's occupation.
15.explanation: Vて-form います is also used in describing a habitual action; that is, when the same action is repeatedly performed over a period of time. Therefore, one's occupation can be expressed by this sentence pattern. If the question おしごとは なんですか is asked, this sentence pattern can be used to answer it.

examples.jp: この会社は コンピューターソフトを 作って います。
examples.en: This company makes computer software.

examples.jp: スーパーで フィルムを 売って います。
examples.en: Supermarkets sell films.

examples.jp: 田中さんは 銀行で 働いて います。
examples.en: Mr. Tanaka works at a bank.

examples.jp: 妹は 大学で 勉強して います。
examples.en: My younger sister is studying at university.

15.summary: Vて-form います also expresses a habitual/repeated action, most commonly used to describe someone's job or field of study.
15.details: The third meaning of ています (alongside progressive action and resulting state) — this habitual-action reading is specifically how Japanese states one's occupation (ABC社で働いています = 'I work for ABC'), a very practical, frequently-used construction worth its own speaking drill.

15.title: 知りません
15.structure: 知って います → 知りません (negative)
15.note: Irregular negative: not 知って いません.
15.meaning: The negative form of 知って います ('know') is the irregular 知りません, not 知って いません.
15.explanation: The negative form of しって います is しりません.

examples.jp: 市役所の 電話番号を 知って いますか。…はい、知って います。…いいえ、知りません。
examples.en: Do you know the telephone number of the city hall? …Yes, I do. …No, I don't.

15.summary: 知っています ('know') has an irregular negative — 知りません, never 知っていません.
15.details: A direct, important exception to the general continuing-state ています pattern: while every other verb in that family negates regularly (結婚していません, 住んでいません are both fine), 知る is the one exception where the plain negative ます-form (知りません) is used instead of the て-form いません negative. Worth flagging clearly since it breaks the otherwise-consistent pattern.

16.title: Vて-form、[Vて-form]、〜
16.meaning: Connects two or more verb sentences in the order the actions occur; tense is determined by the last verb.
16.explanation: To connect verb sentences, the て-form is used. When two or more actions take place in succession, the actions are mentioned in the order of occurrence by using the て-form. The tense of the sentence is determined by the tense form of the last verb in the sentence.

examples.jp: 朝 ジョギングを して、シャワーを 浴びて、会社へ 行きます。
examples.en: In the morning, I jog, take a shower and go to the office.

examples.jp: 神戸へ 行って、映画を 見て、お茶を 飲みました。
examples.en: I went to Kobe, saw a movie and drank tea.

16.summary: Chaining て-forms lists actions in the order they happen; only the final verb's tense governs the whole sentence.
16.details: This extends the て-form beyond requests and ています into another job: connecting a sequence of actions. Since only the last verb carries tense, ました/ます must be judged from the final verb for the earlier ones — a good comprehension check point.

16.title: い-adj(〜い)→〜くて、〜
16.meaning: Joins an い-adjective sentence to another sentence by dropping い and attaching くて ('and').
16.explanation: When joining an い-adjective sentence to another sentence, take away the い from the い-adjective and attach くて. Exception: いい→よくて.

examples.jp: スミスさんは 若くて、元気です。
examples.en: Mr. Smith is young and lively.

examples.jp: きのうは 天気が よくて、暑かったです。
examples.en: Yesterday it was fine and hot.

16.summary: い-adjective + くて links it to a following clause as 'and' — いい is irregular, becoming よくて.
16.details: This mirrors Vて-form chaining, but for い-adjective predicates rather than verbs — くて is the い-adjective's own connective form, parallel to で for nouns/な-adjectives. The いい→よくて irregularity echoes the same exception seen in the past-tense よくなかったです.

16.title: N／な-adj[な]で、〜
16.meaning: Joins noun sentences or な-adjective sentences by changing です to で.
16.explanation: When joining noun sentences or な-adjective sentences, です is changed to で. This can connect sentences with different topics too. This method cannot connect sentences of contradictory notion — が is used instead.

examples.jp: スミスさんは アメリカ人で、京都大学の 留学生です。
examples.en: Mr. Smith is an American and a student of Kyoto University.

examples.jp: スミスさんは ハンサムで、親切です。
examples.en: Mr. Smith is handsome and kind.

examples.jp: 田中さんは 学生で、山本さんは 主婦です。
examples.en: Ms. Tanaka is a student and Ms. Yamamoto is a housewife.

16.summary: N／な-adjective + で joins as 'and' (です→で); for contradictory/contrastive ideas, use が ('but') instead, never で.
16.details: Completes the three-way connective family: verbs use the て-form, い-adjectives use くて, and nouns and な-adjectives use で. The critical warning is that で only works for compatible/additive facts; a contrast (狭いですが、きれいです) must use が, since で cannot carry contradiction.

16.title: V1て-formから、V2
16.meaning: States that V2 is conducted upon completion of V1's action — 'after doing V1.'
16.explanation: This sentence pattern indicates that upon completion of the action denoted by V1, the action of V2 is to be conducted. The tense of the sentence is determined by the tense form of the last verb. The subject of a subordinate clause is indicated by が.

examples.jp: 国へ 帰ってから、父の 会社で 働きます。
examples.en: I will work for my father's company after going back to my country.

examples.jp: コンサートが 終わってから、レストランで 食事しました。
examples.en: We dined at a restaurant after the concert was over.

16.summary: Vて-form + から + V2 = 'after doing V1, V2' — a stronger, explicitly sequential 'after' than plain て-form chaining.
16.details: This is a second job for から, distinct from から (reason) — here it attaches to a て-form to mean 'after,' not 'because.' The subordinate-clause-subject-が note previews a rule that recurs with とき and other subordinate clauses.

16.title: N1は N2が adjective
16.meaning: Describes an attribute of N1 (the topic) via N2 (the subject of the adjective description).
16.explanation: This sentence pattern is used to describe an attribute of a thing or a person. The topic of the sentence is denoted by は. N1 is the topic of the sentence. N2 is the subject of the adjective's description.

examples.jp: 大阪は 食べ物が おいしいです。
examples.en: Food is tasty in Osaka.

examples.jp: 田中さんは 髪が 長いです。
examples.en: Ms. Tanaka has long hair.

16.summary: N1は N2が adjective describes N1's attribute by naming a part/aspect (N2) and an adjective about that part.
16.details: A double-marking pattern that layers は (topic) over が (subject-of-description, familiar from preference/ability sentences) within a single sentence — useful for describing people/places by a specific feature (髪が長い, 食べ物がおいしい) rather than the whole topic directly.

16.title: どうやって
16.meaning: Asks the way or method of doing something; answered using the て-form chaining pattern.
16.explanation: どうやって is used to ask the way or the method of doing something. To answer such a question, the て-form chaining pattern (Vて、Vて、…) is used.

examples.jp: 大学まで どうやって 行きますか。…京都駅から 16番の バスに 乗って、大学前で 降ります。
examples.en: How do you go to your university? …I take a No.16 bus from Kyoto Station and get off at Daigaku-mae.

16.summary: どうやって asks 'by what method/how,' typically answered with a chain of て-form verbs describing the steps.
16.details: Built to be answered using Vて-form chaining — the two work as a matched question/answer pair, much like the から/どうして pairing.

16.title: どの N
16.meaning: Asks the listener to define one among more than two things concretely presented, modifying the following noun.
16.explanation: この、その and あの modify nouns. The interrogative word used in this system is どの. どの is used to ask the listener to define one among more than two which are concretely presented.

examples.jp: スミスさんは どの 人ですか。…あの 背が 高くて、髪が 黒い 人です。
examples.en: Which one is Mr. Smith? …That tall man with black hair is.

16.summary: どの N completes the この/その/あの/どの demonstrative-modifier series, asking the listener to pick out one specific item from several shown.
16.details: Completes the こ/そ/あ/ど demonstrative family alongside どれ (pronoun, stands alone) — どの must be followed by a noun (どの人 'which person'), while どれ stands alone ('which one'). The answer example also uses くて-chaining (背が高くて、髪が黒い).

16.title: そして／それから
16.explanation: そして adds another fact. それから puts events in order, 'and then'.

examples.jp: 朝ごはんを食べました。そして、学校へ行きました。
examples.en: I ate breakfast. And then I went to school.

examples.jp: 宿題をします。それから、テレビを見ます。
examples.en: I'll do homework. After that I'll watch TV.

16.summary: そして adds information; それから stresses the order of events.
16.details: Use それから when the time sequence matters, and そして for plain addition or listing qualities.

17.title: Verb ない-form
17.meaning: The verb form used with ない — the plain negative base form for a family of new negative expressions.
17.explanation: The verb form used with ない is called the ない-form. Group I: replace the final い-line sound of the ます-form with the corresponding あ-line sound (exceptions: 買います/会います use わ, not あ). Group II: same as the ます-form (たべ-ない, み-ない). Group III: します→しない; きます→こない.

examples.jp: かきます → かかない
examples.en: write → nai-form

examples.jp: たべます → たべない
examples.en: eat → nai-form

examples.jp: きます → こない
examples.en: come → nai-form

17.summary: The ない-form is the negative base verb form; Group I swaps ます-stem い-row→あ-row (買う/会う are exceptions, using わ), Group II matches the ます-stem exactly, Group III is irregular (しない, こない).
17.details: A new conjugation base joining the て-form and (later) the た-form as foundational verb forms — the following ない-form patterns all build directly on it, so getting Group I's い→あ shift (and the 買います/会います わ-exception) right is essential.

17.title: Vない-formないで ください
17.structure: Vない-form で ください
17.meaning: Asks or instructs someone not to do something.
17.explanation: This expression is used to ask or instruct someone not to do something.

examples.jp: わたしは 元気ですから、心配しないで ください。
examples.en: I am fine, so please don't worry about me.

examples.jp: ここで 写真を 撮らないで ください。
examples.en: Please don't take pictures here.

17.summary: Vない-form + で + ください (Vないで ください) is the negative counterpart of Vてください — a polite 'please don't.'
17.details: Directly mirrors Vてください (please do), now negated using the ない-form as the base instead of the て-form — worth pairing the two ください patterns together for review as opposites.

17.title: Vない-formなくても いいです
17.structure: Vない-form (drop ない) + なくても いいです
17.meaning: Indicates that the action described by the verb does not have to be done.
17.explanation: This sentence pattern indicates that the action described by the verb does not have to be done.

examples.jp: あした 来なくても いいです。
examples.en: You don't have to come tomorrow.

17.summary: Vない-form + なくても + いいです = 'you don't have to' — the true negation/absence-of-obligation counterpart to なければなりません.
17.details: Together, なければなりません (must) and なくてもいいです (need not) form a complete obligation pair from the ない-form, echoing the permission/prohibition pair Vてもいいです/Vてはいけません — worth drilling all four side by side since the sentence shapes are easy to conflate.

17.title: N(object)は
17.meaning: Replaces を with は to make a direct object the topic of the sentence.
17.explanation: The particle を is attached to the direct object of verbs. Here you learn that the object is made a topic by replacing を with は.

examples.jp: 荷物を ここに 置かないで ください。
examples.en: Please don't put parcels here.

examples.jp: 荷物は ここに 置かないで ください。
examples.en: As for parcels, don't put them here.

examples.jp: 昼ごはんは 会社の 食堂で 食べます。
examples.en: As for lunch, I have it in the company cafeteria.

17.summary: Swapping を for は turns a direct object into the sentence's topic — 'as for [object], ...'
17.details: Builds directly on N を V — this is the object-topicalization counterpart to how time words can take は. A useful general rule: は can replace both が and を when the marked item becomes the topic.

17.title: 〜ちゃいけない／〜なくちゃ
17.structure: V て-form → ちゃ／じゃ + いけない / V ない-form なくちゃ
17.explanation: Casual spoken contractions: てはいけない becomes ちゃいけない, and なくてはいけない becomes なくちゃ.

examples.jp: ここで遊んじゃいけない。
examples.en: You mustn't play here.

examples.jp: もう帰らなくちゃ。
examples.en: I've got to go home now.

17.summary: ちゃ／じゃ and なくちゃ are the relaxed, spoken forms of てはいけない and なくてはいけない.
17.details: て-forms ending in んで／いで (む・ぶ・ぬ・ぐ verbs) use じゃ (遊んじゃ), others use ちゃ (食べちゃ, 書いちゃ). Don't use these contractions in formal writing. They are used in casual speech, so the plain ending いけない is most natural (the polite いけません is a softened spoken variant).

17.title: 〜なくてはいけません／〜なくてはなりません
17.structure: V ない-form (drop い) + くてはいけません／くてはなりません
17.explanation: Another common way to say 'must', equivalent to なければなりません.

examples.jp: 毎日薬を飲まなくてはいけません。
examples.en: I have to take my medicine every day.

examples.jp: 明日までに出さなくてはなりません。
examples.en: It must be handed in by tomorrow.

17.summary: なくてはいけません／なりません mean the same as なければなりません.
17.details: The forms are interchangeable in meaning: なければなりません (more formal), なくてはいけません (everyday), and なくちゃ (casual speech).

18.title: Verb dictionary form
18.meaning: The basic form of a verb, as listed in dictionaries.
18.explanation: This form is the basic form of a verb. Verbs are given in this form in the dictionary, hence the name. Group I: replace the final い-line sound of the ます-form with the corresponding う-line sound. Group II: attach る to the ます-form. Group III: します becomes する; きます becomes くる.

examples.jp: かきます → かく
examples.en: write → dictionary form

examples.jp: たべます → たべる
examples.en: eat → dictionary form

examples.jp: します → する、きます → くる
examples.en: do/come → dictionary form

18.summary: The dictionary form is the plain non-past verb form found in dictionaries — Group I swaps the ます-stem's い-row for う-row, Group II adds る, Group III is irregular (する, くる).
18.details: This is the fourth verb form introduced, after the ます-form, て-form and ない-form — all four are built from the same Group I/II/III classification, so a clear verb-group table across all four forms is worth building as a study aid at this point.

18.title: N／V dictionary form こと が できます
18.structure: N／V dictionary form こと が できます
18.meaning: Expresses ability or possibility — 'can do'; verbs must be nominalized with こと before が できます.
18.explanation: できます is the verb which expresses ability or possibility. A noun and V dictionary form こと before が indicates the content of ability or possibility. Nouns placed before が are mostly nouns which express actions (driving, shopping, skiing, dancing); nouns associated with an action (にほんご with はなす, ピアノ with ひく) can also be used directly.

examples.jp: スミスさんは 日本語が できます。
examples.en: Mr. Smith can speak Japanese.

examples.jp: スミスさんは 漢字を 読む ことが できます。
examples.en: Mr. Smith can read Kanji.

examples.jp: カードで 払う ことが できます。
examples.en: You can pay by credit card.

18.summary: できます (can/be able to) takes が; a bare action-noun can precede it directly, but a verb must first be nominalized into V dictionary form + こと.
18.details: This is the first practical use of the dictionary form: turning a verb into a noun phrase via こと so it can slot into the が-object pattern familiar from preference/ability verbs (which take が). This こと-nominalizer is a general tool for turning verb clauses into nouns.

18.title: わたしの 趣味は N／V dictionary form こと です
18.structure: わたしの 趣味は {N／V dictionary form こと} です
18.meaning: States a hobby, optionally expressed as a full verb phrase nominalized with こと.
18.explanation: V dictionary form こと lets you state the hobby as a concrete activity rather than just a noun.

examples.jp: わたしの 趣味は 音楽です。
examples.en: My hobby is music.

examples.jp: わたしの 趣味は 音楽を 聞く ことです。
examples.en: My hobby is listening to music.

18.summary: 趣味は…こと です applies the こと-nominalizer to state a hobby as a full verb phrase, not just a bare noun.
18.details: A direct practical application of the こと-nominalizer to a new sentence frame (趣味は…です) — reinforces that こと's job is simply 'turn any verb phrase into something a です-sentence or が-clause can hold.'

18.title: V1 dictionary form／Nの／Quantifier(period) まえに、V2
18.meaning: States that V2 happens before V1 (or before a noun-implied action, or a given period of time) — V1 stays in dictionary form regardless of V2's tense.
18.explanation: This sentence pattern indicates that the action of V2 occurs before the action of V1 takes place. Even when the tense of V2 is in the past or future tense, V1 is always in the dictionary form. When まえに comes after a noun, の is inserted (only for nouns implying actions). When まえに comes after a quantifier (period), の is unnecessary.

examples.jp: 日本へ 来る まえに、日本語を 勉強しました。
examples.en: I studied Japanese before I came to Japan.

examples.jp: 食事の まえに、手を 洗います。
examples.en: I wash my hands before eating.

examples.jp: 田中さんは 1時間まえに、出かけました。
examples.en: Mr. Tanaka left an hour ago.

18.summary: [V1 dictionary form／Nの／period]+まえに, V2 = 'before V1, V2' — V1 always stays in the dictionary (non-past) form no matter what tense V2 is in.
18.details: A second major use of the dictionary form, after the こと-nominalizer — here the dictionary form itself (not nominalized) attaches directly to まえに. The tense-invariance rule (V1 is ALWAYS dictionary form) is worth emphasizing, since students may want to match V1's tense to V2's.

19.title: Verb た-form
19.meaning: Formed by changing the て-form's て/で to た/だ respectively.
19.explanation: The た-form is made by changing て and で of the て-form into た and だ respectively.

examples.jp: かいて → かいた
examples.en: write (て-form → た-form)

examples.jp: のんで → のんだ
examples.en: drink (て-form → た-form)

examples.jp: たべて → たべた
examples.en: eat (て-form → た-form)

19.summary: The た-form (plain past) is derived mechanically from the て-form by swapping て/で for た/だ — the last of the basic verb forms.
19.details: Completes the set of core verb forms alongside ます-form, て-form, ない-form and dictionary form — since it's built directly from the て-form students already know, it's the easiest to produce once て-form is solid.

19.title: Vた-form ことが あります
19.structure: Vた-form ことが あります
19.meaning: Describes what one has experienced in the past, distinct from simply stating a past fact.
19.explanation: This sentence pattern is used to describe what one has experienced in the past. This is basically the same sentence as わたしは Nが あります (have/own N). The content of one's experience is expressed by the nominalized phrase Vた-form こと.

examples.jp: 馬に 乗った ことが あります。
examples.en: I have ridden a horse.

examples.jp: 去年 北海道で 馬に 乗りました。
examples.en: I rode a horse in Hokkaido last year. (plain past fact, for contrast)

19.summary: Vた-form + ことが あります states 'I have the experience of having done X' — distinct from a plain past-tense statement of a single occurrence (Vました).
19.details: Combines the た-form with the こと-nominalizer, slotted into the が あります pattern — a clean example of how these building blocks recombine. The contrast example makes clear this is about lifetime experience, not a single dated event.

19.title: Vた-formり、Vた-formり します
19.meaning: Lists a few representative actions out of many, without implying a fixed time order between them.
19.explanation: You already know an expression for referring to a few things and persons among many (〜や〜[など]). The sentences here are used in referring to some actions among many other actions. The tense of this sentence pattern is shown at the end of the sentence.

examples.jp: 日曜日は テニスを したり、映画を 見たり します。
examples.en: On Sundays I play tennis, see a movie and so on.

examples.jp: 先週の 日曜日は テニスを して、映画を 見ました。
examples.en: Last Sunday I played tennis and then saw a movie. (contrast with plain て-form: implies sequence)

19.summary: Vた-form+り、Vた-form+り+します lists representative actions (no fixed order implied), just as や does for nouns — contrast with plain て-form chaining, which does imply sequence.
19.details: Directly parallels や (representative nouns) but for verbs — and explicitly contrasts with て-form chaining, which DOES imply a time sequence. This たり／たり construction breaks that sequence implication, listing activities as loose examples instead.

19.title: い-adj(〜い)→〜く／な-adj[な]→に／N に なります
19.structure: {い-adj(〜い)→〜く／な-adj[な]→に／Nに} なります
19.meaning: なります means 'become' and indicates changes in a state or condition.
19.explanation: なります means 'become' and indicates changes in a state or condition.

examples.jp: 寒い → 寒く なります
examples.en: get cold

examples.jp: 元気[な] → 元気に なります
examples.en: get well

examples.jp: 25歳 → 25歳に なります
examples.en: become 25 years old

19.summary: い-adjective→く, な-adjective/noun→に, both + なります express a change of state ('become cold/well/25 years old').
19.details: い-adjectives drop the final い and add く; な-adjectives and nouns add に — then なります follows. Note the same い→く / な・N→に split appears in other adjective-to-adverb conversions, so it is worth learning as one pattern.

19.title: そうですね
19.note: Contrast with そうですか (falling intonation).
19.meaning: Used to agree or sympathize with what your conversation partner said.
19.explanation: そうですね is used when you agree or sympathize with what your partner in conversation said. そうですか with a falling intonation is a similar expression to this, but is an expression of one's conviction or exclamation after getting information which was unknown to you, while そうですね is used to express one's agreement or sympathy with one's partner when he/she refers to something you agree with or already know.

examples.jp: 寒く なりましたね。…そうですね。
examples.en: It's got cold, hasn't it? …Yes, it has.

19.summary: そうですね agrees/sympathizes with something the listener already shares/knows; そうですか(falling tone) instead marks newly-learned information — a subtle but important pragmatic distinction.
19.details: Contrasts with the acknowledgment そうですか ('I see') — そうですね requires shared/agreed information, そうですか(↘) marks brand-new information just received. Good candidate for a listening-discrimination drill since intonation is the only surface difference from そうですか(↗)'s confirming-question use.

20.title: Polite style and plain style
20.structure: polite style (です／ます) vs. plain style (だ／dictionary, た-form, ない-form)
20.meaning: Japanese has two speech styles: predicates ending in です/ます are the polite style; their plain equivalents are the plain style.
20.explanation: Japanese language has two styles of speech: polite style and plain style. The predicates which are used in polite style sentences and accompanied by either です or ます are called the polite form, while the predicates used in plain style sentences are called the plain form.

examples.jp: あした 東京へ 行きます。／あした 東京へ 行く。
examples.en: I will go to Tokyo tomorrow. (polite / plain)

examples.jp: 相撲が 好きです。／相撲が 好きだ。
examples.en: I like sumo. (polite / plain)

examples.jp: ドイツへ 行った ことが ありません。／ドイツへ 行った ことが ない。
examples.en: I have never been to Germany. (polite / plain)

20.summary: Every sentence has a polite form (です／ます) and a plain form (だ／dictionary-ない-た-forms) — the plain forms are exactly the dictionary, ない- and た-forms already learned, used as sentence-final predicates instead of building blocks.
20.details: This reveals that the dictionary, ない and た forms learned so far are actually the plain-style equivalents of ます/ません/ました — they were being taught as building blocks first, and only now get explicitly named as the plain predicate style. A genuine 'aha' moment worth highlighting.

20.title: Proper use of the polite style or the plain style
20.meaning: The polite style is used with strangers, superiors, and people not close to you; the plain style is used with close friends, colleagues, and family, and is standard in most written work.
20.explanation: The polite style can be used at anytime in any place and to anybody — used most commonly between adults who are not close friends, when talking to someone met for the first time, to superiors, or to people not very close even in a similar age group. The plain style is used with close friends, colleagues and family members. If unsure, it is safer to use the polite style. The plain style is common in written work (newspapers, books, theses, diaries); most letters are written in the polite style.

examples.jp: （会話）友達に：元気？　…うん、元気。
examples.en: (casual, to a close friend) How are you? …Fine.

20.summary: Choose polite style by default (safe with strangers/superiors/not-close acquaintances); reserve plain style for close friends/family, and expect it in most written Japanese except letters.
20.details: A sociolinguistic/register point rather than a new sentence pattern — directly informs when to actually deploy the plain forms and plain-style conversation habits. The 'when in doubt, use polite' guidance is worth remembering as a safety default.

20.title: Conversation in the plain style
20.note: Multiple sub-rules: か dropped with rising intonation; だ dropped/softened; other particles often dropped; いる's い often dropped; けど as a casual が.
20.meaning: A set of conversational habits that mark casual plain-style speech: omitting か (using rising intonation instead), omitting/softening だ, dropping certain particles when context is clear, dropping い from ている/でいる, and using けど as a casual equivalent of が.
20.explanation: 1) Questions in the plain style generally omit か and end with rising intonation. 2) In noun/な-adjective questions, だ (the plain form of です) is omitted; in an affirmative answer だ can be omitted or softened with a sentence-final particle — women seldom use だ. 3) Particles are often omitted if the meaning is clear from context, but で、に、から、まで、と are not omitted. 4) い of Vて-form いる is often dropped. 5) けど has the same function as が (connecting two sentences) and is common in conversation.

examples.jp: コーヒーを 飲む？…うん、飲む。
examples.en: Do you want a coffee? …Yes, I do. (the question has rising intonation)

examples.jp: ごはん[を] 食べる？
examples.en: Are you going to eat?

examples.jp: 辞書、持って[い]る？…うん、持って[い]る。
examples.en: Do you have a dictionary? …Yes, I do.

examples.jp: そのカレーライス[は] おいしい？…うん、辛いけど、おいしい。
examples.en: Is that curry and rice tasty? …Yes, it's hot but tasty.

20.summary: Casual plain-style conversation drops か (rising tone instead), often drops だ, drops most particles except で/に/から/まで/と, drops い from ている, and uses けど as a casual が.
20.details: This ties together several threads: だ is the plain copula; けど reuses が's connective job in a more colloquial register; the ている→てる contraction (dropping い) is a very common real-world speech feature. Together, the plain-style points form one cohesive 'register' topic worth reviewing as a unit rather than as separate grammar points.

20.title: 〜だろう
20.structure: V／い-adj plain form、な-adj stem／N + だろう
20.explanation: The plain-style counterpart of でしょう: the speaker thinks something is probably true.

examples.jp: 明日は雨が降るだろう。
examples.en: It will probably rain tomorrow.

examples.jp: 彼はもう帰っただろう。
examples.en: He has probably gone home already.

20.summary: だろう is the plain form of でしょう, expressing probability.
20.details: だろう appears in plain-style writing and male casual speech; だろうか (I wonder?) and だろう? (right?) are common variants. Polite speech uses でしょう.

21.title: V／い-adj／な-adj／N plain form でしょう？
21.structure: {V／い-adj／な-adj／N} plain form でしょう？
21.meaning: Used when the speaker expects the listener to share some knowledge and agree with the speaker's view.
21.explanation: When the speaker expects that the listener has some knowledge on the topic being discussed and that the listener will agree with the speaker's view, でしょう is said with a rising intonation to confirm the listener's agreement.

examples.jp: あした パーティーに 行くでしょう？…ええ、行きます。
examples.en: You are going to the party tomorrow, aren't you? …Yes, I am.

examples.jp: 北海道は 寒かったでしょう？…いいえ、そんなに 寒くなかったです。
examples.en: It was cold in Hokkaido, wasn't it? …No, it wasn't that cold.

21.summary: Plain form + でしょう？(rising tone) seeks the listener's agreement/confirmation on something the speaker assumes they already know — 'right?' / 'wasn't it?'
21.details: This でしょう builds on plain forms and functions much like English tag questions ('..., isn't it?'). Distinct from the plain でしょう statement (falling tone, meaning 'probably') that appears without a question mark elsewhere — intonation alone distinguishes the confirmation-seeking use here.

21.title: N1(place)で N2が あります
21.structure: N1(place)で N2が あります
21.meaning: で marks the place where an event (party, concert, festival, incident, disaster) takes place, when N2 means 'to be held/take place.'
21.explanation: When N2 expresses such events as a party, concert, festival, incident, disaster and so on, あります means 'to take place' or 'to be held.'

examples.jp: 東京で 日本と ブラジルの サッカーの 試合が あります。
examples.en: A football game between Japan and Brazil will be held in Tokyo.

21.summary: N1(place)で N2(event)が あります states that an event is held/takes place at a location — a special event-related meaning of あります distinct from its plain existence meaning.
21.details: Reuses で as place-of-action (contrasted with に as place-of-existence) — here で marks where an event happens, and あります itself takes on the special 'be held/take place' sense rather than its usual 'exist' meaning.

21.title: N(occasion)で
21.meaning: で marks the occasion on which some action takes place.
21.explanation: When some action takes place on a certain occasion, that occasion is followed by で.

examples.jp: 会議で 何か 意見を 言いましたか。
examples.en: Did you give your opinion at the meeting?

21.summary: で after an occasion-noun (会議で, パーティーで) marks the setting/occasion in which an action occurs.
21.details: Yet another job for で, alongside place-of-action and tool/means — で keeps accumulating uses; worth maintaining a running list of で's jobs (place, means, occasion, and connective) as a single reference.

21.title: N でも V
21.meaning: でも gives an example out of things of the same kind, used when encouraging, advising, or suggesting.
21.explanation: でも is used to give an example out of things of the same kind (e.g. drinks) when one encourages or advises someone to do something or when one makes a suggestion.

examples.jp: ちょっと ビールでも 飲みませんか。
examples.en: Shall we drink beer or something?

21.summary: Nでも V softens a suggestion by presenting N as just one example from a category ('beer or something'), rather than a strict demand.
21.details: A pragmatically softening use of でも, distinct from its more common 'even' meaning — worth flagging since でも here doesn't mean 'even beer' but rather 'beer, for example (among other options).'

22.title: Noun modification
22.note: Review of single-word and short-phrase modifiers.
22.meaning: Recaps that whatever modifies a noun — word or sentence — always precedes it in Japanese.
22.explanation: You already know how to modify nouns with の (スミスさんの うち) and with adjectives (新しい うち, きれいな うち). In Japanese, whatever modifies a word, whether it's a word or a sentence, always comes before the word to be modified.

examples.jp: スミスさんの うち
examples.en: Mr. Smith's house

examples.jp: 新しい うち
examples.en: a new house

examples.jp: きれいな うち
examples.en: a beautiful house

22.summary: Simple noun modification (N の N, い-adjective N, な-adjective な N) always places the modifier before the noun — this principle extends to whole sentences (see noun modification by sentences).
22.details: A deliberate recap tying together adjective+noun and the possessive の, setting up the much bigger leap: a full sentence, not just a word, modifying a noun the same way.

22.title: Noun modification by sentences
22.meaning: A relative clause (whole sentence in plain form) can modify a noun, just like a single adjective — な-adjective だ→な, noun だ→の in this position.
22.explanation: The predicate of the sentence which modifies a noun is in the plain form. In the case of な-adjective sentences, 〜だ becomes 〜な; in noun sentences 〜だ becomes 〜の. Nouns which are elements of the sentence (object, place, indirect object) can also be modified by relativizing around them — the particles を、で、に attached to them become unnecessary. The noun modified by such a sentence can be used in various parts of a larger sentence.

examples.jp: 京都へ 行った 人
examples.en: a person who went to Kyoto

examples.jp: 背が 高くて、髪が 黒い 人
examples.en: a person who is tall and has black hair

examples.jp: わたしは 先週 映画を 見ました → わたしが 先週 見た 映画
examples.en: I saw a movie last week → the movie that I saw last week

examples.jp: これは スミスさんが 住んで いた うちです。
examples.en: This is the house where Mr. Smith lived.

22.summary: A whole clause in plain form can precede and modify a noun like a relative clause ('the movie [that] I saw', 'the house where Mr. Smith lived'); な-adjective/noun predicates take な/の instead of だ, and the relativized noun's original particle (を/で/に) is dropped.
22.details: This is the single biggest new structure at this stage — relative clauses. It depends on the plain forms (だ→な/の adjustment for nouns/な-adjectives) and reuses が for the subject inside the modifying clause. Worth extensive drilling since English speakers instinctively want a relative pronoun (like 'that'/'which') that Japanese simply omits.

22.title: Nが (subject of a modifying sentence)
22.structure: Nが V／adjective, inside a noun-modifying clause
22.meaning: When a sentence modifies a noun, the subject within that modifying sentence is marked with が (not は).
22.explanation: When a sentence modifies a noun, the subject in the sentence is indicated by が.

examples.jp: スミスさんは ケーキを 作りました。→ これは スミスさんが 作った ケーキです。
examples.en: Mr. Smith baked a cake. → This is the cake which Mr. Smith baked.

examples.jp: わたしは たなかさんが かいた 絵が 好きです。
examples.en: I like the picture that Ms. Tanaka drew.

examples.jp: [あなたは] 彼が 生まれた 所を 知って いますか。
examples.en: Do you know the place where he was born?

22.summary: Inside a relative (noun-modifying) clause, the subject normally takes が (or の), even though it would take は as the topic of a standalone sentence.
22.details: This is a critical companion rule to noun modification by sentences: when a full sentence like スミスさんは…作りました becomes a modifier (スミスさんが作った), は switches to が. This は→が shift inside subordinate clauses echoes the same subject-marking rule seen with から and will recur with とき and conditionals.

22.title: V dictionary form 時間／約束／用事
22.structure: V dictionary form + 時間／約束／用事
22.meaning: Puts the dictionary form of an action before じかん/やくそく/ようじ to express the time for, arrangement for, or thing to do regarding that action.
22.explanation: When expressing the time for doing some activity, put the dictionary form of the action before じかん. You can also say the content of the arrangement (appointment) by putting the dictionary form of that action before やくそく, etc.

examples.jp: わたしは 朝ごはんを 食べる 時間が ありません。
examples.en: I have no time to eat breakfast.

examples.jp: わたしは 友達と 映画を 見る 約束が あります。
examples.en: I have an arrangement to see a movie with a friend of mine.

examples.jp: きょうは 市役所へ 行く 用事が あります。
examples.en: I have something to do at the city hall today.

22.summary: V dictionary form directly modifies 時間/約束/用事 (time/appointment/errand) as a noun-modifying clause, specifying what the time/appointment/errand is for.
22.details: A specific, very useful application of noun modification by sentences — exactly the same relative-clause mechanism, just restricted to a small set of practical nouns (時間, 約束, 用事) that describe scheduled activities.

23.title: V dictionary form／Vない-form／い-adj／な-adjな／Nの とき、〜
23.structure: {V dictionary form／Vない-form／い-adj(〜い)／な-adjな／Nの} とき、〜
23.meaning: とき connects two sentences, expressing the time when the state or action in the main sentence exists/occurs; the modifying forms match noun-modification rules.
23.explanation: とき connects two sentences and expresses the time when the state or action described in the main sentence exists or occurs. As shown in noun-modification rules, the forms of verbs, い-adjectives, な-adjectives and nouns connected to とき are the same as the forms when modifying nouns. The tense of adjective sentences and noun sentences which modify とき is not affected by the tense of the main sentence.

examples.jp: 図書館で 本を 借りる とき、カードが 要ります。
examples.en: When you borrow books from the library, you need a card.

examples.jp: 暇な とき、うちへ 遊びに 来ませんか。
examples.en: Won't you come to my place when you are free?

examples.jp: 子どもの とき、よく 川で 泳ぎました。
examples.en: I used to swim in a river when I was a child.

23.summary: とき ('when') attaches after the same plain/modifying forms used for noun modification — い-adjective plain, な-adjective+な, noun+の, verb dictionary/ない-form — and its own tense is independent of the main clause's tense for adjective/noun とき-clauses.
23.details: This directly reuses the noun-modification forms (だ→な/の for nouns and な-adjectives) — とき is essentially treated as a noun being modified by the preceding clause ('at the time that...'), which is why the same modification rules apply.

23.title: V dictionary form／Vた-form とき、〜
23.note: Dictionary form = not yet completed; た-form = already completed.
23.meaning: Whether とき is preceded by the dictionary form or the た-form of a verb changes whether the action is non-completed or completed at the time referred to.
23.explanation: When the dictionary form of the predicate is put before とき it indicates the non-completion of the action, and when the た-form of the predicate is put before とき it indicates the completion of the action.

examples.jp: 国へ 帰る とき、かばんを 買いました。
examples.en: I bought a bag when I went back to my country. (before returning — bought abroad)

examples.jp: 国へ 帰った とき、かばんを 買いました。
examples.en: I bought a bag when I went back to my country. (after returning — bought at home)

23.summary: Vとき uses dictionary form when the とき-verb's action is NOT YET completed at the reference time, and た-form when it IS already completed — the same verb pair can produce two different real-world meanings.
23.details: A subtle but important refinement of とき for verbs specifically — this dictionary-form/た-form contrast doesn't exist for adjectives or nouns in とき-clauses (which aren't tense-sensitive), making verb-とき uniquely two-directional. Worth a dedicated comprehension exercise contrasting both readings of the identical example sentence.

23.title: Nが adjective／V (state or scene as it is)
23.note: Extends the natural-phenomenon が rule to any state/scene description.
23.meaning: When describing a state or scene as it is (not just natural phenomena), the subject is also indicated by が.
23.explanation: The subject is indicated by が when describing a natural phenomenon. When describing a state or a scene as it is, the subject is also indicated by が.

examples.jp: 音が 小さいです。
examples.en: The volume is low.

examples.jp: 電気が 明るく なりました。
examples.en: The light became brighter.

examples.jp: このボタンを 押すと、切符が 出ます。
examples.en: Press this button, and a ticket will come out.

23.summary: が marks the subject not only for natural phenomena but for any plain description of a state or scene as it presents itself — a broadening of the same underlying rule.
23.details: Direct extension of natural-phenomenon が (雨が降っています) — the rule generalizes from weather specifically to any observed state/scene (音が小さい, 電気が明るくなりました), reinforcing が's role for 'new information being reported/observed' rather than は's role for 'topic already under discussion.'

23.title: N(place)を V(verb of movement)
23.meaning: を marks the place a person or thing passes through/along, used with verbs of movement (さんぽします, わたります, あるきます, etc.).
23.explanation: The particle を is used to denote the place where a person or a thing passes. The verb of movement such as さんぽします、わたります、あるきます、etc. are used in this pattern.

examples.jp: 公園を 散歩します。
examples.en: I take a walk in the park.

examples.jp: 道を 渡ります。
examples.en: I cross the road.

examples.jp: 交差点を 右へ 曲がります。
examples.en: I turn to the right at the intersection.

23.summary: を after a place noun, with a movement verb (歩く, 渡る, 散歩する, 曲がる), marks the path/route being traversed — a third role for を beyond direct object and departure point.
23.details: This is yet another job for を, joining direct object and departure point (でます/おります) — を's overall pattern is: direct object, point of departure, and now path traversed. Good candidate for a summary review of を's several distinct roles.

24.title: くれます
24.meaning: Used when somebody else gives something to the speaker or the speaker's family — あげます cannot be used in this direction.
24.explanation: あげます means 'give' (the giver is the speaker or someone near the speaker's side). This verb cannot be used when somebody else gives something to the speaker or the speaker's family, etc. (×たなかさんは わたしに クリスマスカードを あげました is wrong). In this case くれます is used.

examples.jp: わたしは たなかさんに 花を あげました。
examples.en: I gave flowers to Ms. Tanaka.

examples.jp: たなかさんは わたしに クリスマスカードを くれました。
examples.en: Ms. Tanaka gave me a Christmas card.

examples.jp: たなかさんは 妹に お菓子を くれました。
examples.en: Ms. Tanaka gave candies to my younger sister.

24.summary: くれます means 'give,' used specifically when someone else gives something TO the speaker (or the speaker's in-group) — あげます cannot be used in that direction.
24.details: Completes the giving/receiving verb family alongside あげます (I give to others) and もらいます (I receive from others) — くれます fills the missing direction: someone else gives to me. The three verbs together (あげる/もらう/くれる) form the core of Japanese's perspective-sensitive giving-verb system.

24.title: N(person)が V
24.note: が introduces new information about who did something, in response to a topic already raised.
24.meaning: The subject of a sentence giving new information (in response to a raised topic) is indicated by が.
24.explanation: You present a topic (e.g. commenting on a tie); your partner's response gives a piece of information on the topic which is unknown to you — the subject of the sentence giving that new information is indicated by が.

examples.jp: すてきな ネクタイですね。…ええ、たなかさんが くれました。
examples.en: That's a nice tie, isn't it? …Yes. Ms. Tanaka gave it to me.

24.summary: When a response supplies new information about who did something (in reply to an observation/topic already raised), that subject takes が, not は.
24.details: Reinforces the recurring theme across the course that が marks new/unknown information while は marks an established topic — this specific conversational pattern (comment → が-marked answer revealing the actor) is a natural, frequent real-life usage worth roleplaying.

24.title: Interrogative が V
24.meaning: When the subject of a verb sentence is questioned, it is marked with が, same as for あります/います and adjective sentences.
24.explanation: When the subject is questioned, it is indicated by が in あります/います sentences and adjective sentences. This is also the case for verb sentences.

examples.jp: だれが 手伝いに 行きますか。…スミスさんが 行きます。
examples.en: Who will go to help? …Ms. Smith will.

24.summary: An interrogative subject (だれが, 何が) always takes が, whether the sentence is あります/います, an adjective sentence, or, as confirmed here, an ordinary verb sentence.
24.details: A tidy closing generalization: this rule applies to existence sentences and adjective sentences too, and is now confirmed to apply universally to verb sentences — good to state explicitly as 'interrogative subjects always take が' as a single memorizable rule covering all three cases.

25.title: Nが (subject of a subordinate clause)
25.structure: Nが, inside a たら／ても／とき／まえに-clause
25.note: Generalizes the subordinate-clause-subject-が rule across から, とき and まえに clauses.
25.meaning: The subject of a subordinate clause is indicated by が, as with a から-clause.
25.explanation: As with the subject of a から-clause, the subject of a subordinate clause is indicated by が. In subordinate clauses using たら、ても、とき、と、まえに、etc., in addition to から, the subject is indicated by が, as shown below.

examples.jp: 友達が 来る まえに、部屋を 掃除します。
examples.en: I will clean my room before my friends come.

examples.jp: 妻が 病気の とき、会社を 休みます。
examples.en: When my wife is sick, I take a day off work.

examples.jp: 友達が 約束の 時間に 来なかったら、どう しますか。
examples.en: If your friend doesn't come on time, what will you do?

25.summary: が typically marks the subject inside a subordinate clause — から, とき, と, まえに, たら/ても — a single unifying rule for a pattern seen piecemeal across many structures.
25.details: This is an explicit summary of a rule that has been quietly appearing throughout — a good checkpoint to consolidate: whenever a clause is subordinate (attached before から/とき/と/まえに/たら/ても), its subject typically takes が even if the same sentence standing alone would use は.
